# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): it always plays the fixed level, because the
  random generator recursed to ~315 KB and boot-looped the board, and the
  ghosts' route search is a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Each patch checks
  what it replaces. Its sprite sheet is built from `vendor/` into the build dir
  by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps; ideas for more are in issue #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass, `nm`
  still shows soft-double helpers in Euler2D, Halftone, Interaggregate and
  Anemone; their source was not chased.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that

/* Shim replacement for xscreensaver's utils/ximage-loader.h. Not derived from
 * xscreensaver code.
 *
 * Upstream decodes a PNG. The device has no decoder, so the "image data" here
 * is a raw blob made on the Mac by tools/make_logo_blob.py:
 *
 *   bytes 0-3          the characters "565M"
 *   bytes 4-5          width, unsigned 16-bit little-endian
 *   bytes 6-7          height, unsigned 16-bit little-endian
 *   next width*height  pixels, row by row, each RGB565 as 16-bit little-endian
 *   remainder          mask, row by row, each row padded to whole bytes,
 *                      most significant bit first; 1 = draw the pixel
 *
 * The blob size must match its width and height exactly. */
#ifndef XSHIM_XIMAGE_LOADER_H
#define XSHIM_XIMAGE_LOADER_H

#include "x11shim/xshim.h"

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif

/* Returns a colour pixmap, and writes its size and a depth-1 mask pixmap
 * through the pointers. Returns None (and writes zeros and None) when the
 * blob is not valid or memory runs out. The caller frees both pixmaps. */
Pixmap image_data_to_pixmap(Display *, Window, const unsigned char *data,
                            unsigned long size, int *width_ret,
                            int *height_ret, Pixmap *mask_ret);

/* Upstream reads an image file. The device has no filesystem for hacks and no
 * decoder, so this always returns NULL, and a hack that loads an optional
 * picture carries on without one. */
XImage *file_to_ximage(Display *, Visual *, const char *filename);

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

#endif

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.13"
# dependencies = ["pillow"]
# ///
"""Turn an image into the C header that Maze's logo is read from.

The device has no PNG decoder, so the image goes in as a raw RGB565 blob with
a 1-bit mask. The layout is documented in
firmware/src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h.

Run with: uv run tools/make_logo_blob.py logo-50.gif --name logo_50_png \\
    -o firmware/src/x11shim/include/images/gen/logo-50_png.h
"""

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

OPAQUE_ALPHA = 128


def rgb565(r: int, g: int, b: int) -> int:
    return (r & 0xF8) << 8 | (g & 0xFC) << 3 | b >> 3


def build_blob(width: int, height: int, rgba: bytes) -> bytes:
    if not (0 < width <= 0xFFFF and 0 < height <= 0xFFFF):
        raise ValueError(f"size {width}x{height} does not fit the blob header")
    if len(rgba) != width * height * 4:
        raise ValueError(f"expected {width * height * 4} RGBA bytes, got {len(rgba)}")

    pixels = bytearray()
    mask = bytearray()
    stride = (width + 7) // 8
    for y in range(height):
        row = bytearray(stride)
        for x in range(width):
            r, g, b, a = rgba[(y * width + x) * 4 :][:4]
            opaque = a >= OPAQUE_ALPHA
            pixels += (rgb565(r, g, b) if opaque else 0).to_bytes(2, "little")

"""PlatformIO pre-build script: converts xscreensaver's pacman.png into the
raw blob pacman.c includes as images/gen/pacman_png.h (see
src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h for the format) and puts it on the include
path. The image is read from vendor/ and never committed; its header is
3 MB of C text. Needs uv, because Pillow is not in PlatformIO's Python."""

import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

Import("env")  # noqa: F821

repo = Path(env["PROJECT_DIR"]).parent  # noqa: F821
image = repo / "vendor" / "xscreensaver-6.16" / "hacks" / "images" / "pacman.png"
converter = repo / "tools" / "make_logo_blob.py"
generated = Path(env.subst("$BUILD_DIR")) / "generated"  # noqa: F821
header = generated / "images" / "gen" / "pacman_png.h"

if not image.is_file():
    sys.exit(f"{image} is missing: run `uv run tools/fetch_xscreensaver.py`")
if (
    not header.exists()
    or header.stat().st_mtime < image.stat().st_mtime
    or header.stat().st_mtime < converter.stat().st_mtime
):
    uv = shutil.which("uv")
    if not uv:
        sys.exit("pacman_sprites.py needs uv on PATH to convert pacman.png")
    header.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Written beside the header and renamed, so a killed build never leaves a
    # truncated header that the mtime check above would trust.
    partial = header.with_name(header.name + ".partial")
    partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    subprocess.run(
        [uv, "run", str(converter), str(image), "--name", "pacman_png", "-o", str(partial)],
        check=True,
    )
    os.replace(partial, header)

env.Append(CPPPATH=[str(generated)])  # noqa: F821

        mask += row
    header = b"565M" + width.to_bytes(2, "little") + height.to_bytes(2, "little")
    return bytes(header + pixels + mask)


def c_header(name: str, blob: bytes, source: str) -> str:
    guard = f"XSHIM_{name.upper()}_H"
    lines = []
    for i in range(0, len(blob), 12):
        lines.append("    " + ", ".join(f"0x{b:02x}" for b in blob[i : i + 12]) + ",")
    body = "\n".join(lines)
    return (
        f"/* Generated by tools/make_logo_blob.py from {source}; do not edit.\n"
        " * Despite the name (maze.c asks for a PNG), this is the raw blob\n"
        " * described in ximage-loader.h. */\n"
        f"#ifndef {guard}\n"
        f"#define {guard}\n"
        f"static const unsigned char {name}[] = {{\n"
        f"{body}\n"
        "};\n"
        "#endif\n"
    )


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    from PIL import Image

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n\n")[0])
    parser.add_argument("image")
    parser.add_argument("--name", required=True, help="C array name")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", required=True)
    parser.add_argument(
        "--size",
        type=int,
        help="shrink to fit this many pixels square, keeping the aspect ratio "
        "(never enlarges)",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

cd /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/firmware && cat > matrix_glyphs.py <<'E'
"""PlatformIO pre-build script: converts xscreensaver's four xmatrix glyph
sheets (matrix1, matrix1b, matrix2, matrix2b) into the raw blobs xmatrix.c
includes as images/gen/<name>_png.h (see src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h
for the format) and puts them on the include path. The images are read from
vendor/ and never committed. Needs uv, because Pillow is not in PlatformIO's
Python."""

import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

Import("env")  # noqa: F821

repo = Path(env["PROJECT_DIR"]).parent  # noqa: F821
images = repo / "vendor" / "xscreensaver-6.16" / "hacks" / "images"
converter = repo / "tools" / "make_logo_blob.py"
generated = Path(env.subst("$BUILD_DIR")) / "generated"  # noqa: F821

for name in ("matrix1", "matrix1b", "matrix2", "matrix2b"):
    image = images / f"{name}.png"
    header = generated / "images" / "gen" / f"{name}_png.h"
    if not image.is_file():
        sys.exit(f"{image} is missing: run `uv run tools/fetch_xscreensaver.py`")
    if (
        header.exists()
        and header.stat().st_mtime >= image.stat().st_mtime
        and header.stat().st_mtime >= converter.stat().st_mtime
    ):
        continue
    uv = shutil.which("uv")
    if not uv:
        sys.exit("matrix_glyphs.py needs uv on PATH to convert the glyph sheets")
    header.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Written beside the header and renamed, so a killed build never leaves a
    # truncated header that the mtime check above would trust.
    partial = header.with_name(header.name + ".partial")
    partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    subprocess.run(
        [uv, "run", str(converter), str(image), "--name", f"{name}_png", "-o", str(partial)],
        check=True,
    )
    os.replace(partial, header)

env.Append(CPPPATH=[str(generated)])  # noqa: F821
E
python3 - <<'E'
p='platformio.ini'; s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("pre:pacman_sprites.py,","pre:pacman_sprites.py, pre:matrix_glyphs.py,")
open(p,'w').write(s); print(s.count("pre:matrix_glyphs.py"))
E

content.content:
## Measured on the device

Fifty-three hacks have been run so far (default settings, 466×466 canvas
pushed to the display every frame, canvas held in PSRAM). The firmware times
each frame in three parts, averaged over 5 seconds: **step** is the hack's own
draw call, **push** is sending the canvas to the display, and **wait** is what
is left of the delay the hack asked for once the push is credited against it
(the runner caps any delay at 10 seconds). Rows other than Rorschach and Pedal
were measured before the cap was raised from 1 second; Helix also asks for
5-second holds, so its frame rate will now be lower than shown.

| Hack | fps | step | push | wait | Extra PSRAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pyro | 30.0 | 0.8-1.1 ms | 31.2 ms | 0 ms | about 80 KB |
| HyperCube | 28.3 | 2.7-2.9 ms | 31.5 ms | 0 ms | none measurable |
| Petri | 28.8-30.8 | 0.3-2.5 ms | 31.1 ms | 0 ms | about 1.3 MB |
| XSpirograph | 11.0-11.4 | 54-56 ms | 31.4 ms | 0-20 ms | none measurable |
| Helix | 16.6-23.6 | 0.9-2.1 ms | 31.3 ms | 9-26 ms | none measurable |
| Rorschach | 3.0 | 0.6-1.7 ms | 31.1-31.2 ms | 367 ms | none measurable |
| Pedal | 0.2-0.4 | 126-519 ms | 31.4-31.5 ms | 3290-5507 ms | none measurable |
| Coral | 15.0-21.2 | 15-25 ms | 31.2 ms | 0-10 ms | about 240 KB |
| Squiral | 30.6-31.0 | 0.1-0.3 ms | 31.1 ms | 0 ms | about 850 KB |
| Critical | 30.4 | 0.7 ms | 31.1 ms | 0 ms | about 15 KB |
| CloudLife | 24.2 | 8.8-8.9 ms | 31.4 ms | 0 ms | about 260 KB |
| WhirlWindWarp | 17.0-24.8 | 6.2-26.4 ms | 31.3 ms | 0 ms | about 410 KB |
| Flame | 4.4-6.8 | 26-107 ms | 31.3-31.4 ms | 85-187 ms | none measurable |
| Hopalong | 19.2-25.2 | 7.3-20.1 ms | 31.2-31.3 ms | 0 ms | about 8 KB |
| Vines | 2.8-3.0 | 133-160 ms | 31.2 ms | 175-187 ms | none measurable |
| Sierpinski | 2.4-2.6 | 1.8-4.0 ms | 31.3-31.4 ms | 377-409 ms | about 32 KB |
| FadePlot | 28.0-28.2 | 2.9-3.2 ms | 31.3-31.4 ms | 0 ms | about 16 KB |
  The polyline path also leaves gaps in a ring, which the ring does not.
- Translucency is a per-GC `alpha` (26 of 32, the weight upstream's
  translucent path uses) that `stroke.c` blends over the canvas. Blending each
  piece of a polyline separately blended the overlaps twice, so a star's
  corners showed as bright diamonds (11.2-13.2 fps). Drawing a translucent
  shape into a one-bit-per-pixel mask and blending it once removed them, and
  costs 3-5 ms a frame on the board (10.4-12.8 fps) though nothing on the
  host. That is the registered build.
- Not measured: PSRAM against an idle build (it was flat at 7,327,227 in every
  capture, so the 27 KB mask per shape is returned), a restart or lap soak
  with rotation on, and a long run. Heap held at 322,648-323,056 bytes.
  Colour was judged by Rod on the screen.

Unknown Pleasures' rows are from pinned builds (2026-10-10). The first flash
had TinyGL's one-pixel lines and its additive blend, so the black quads that
should hide the rows behind a peak hid nothing; the registered row is after
smooth lines, opaque fills, polygon offset and the refresh-synced push (see the
GL notes and `.claude/rules/device-display.md`). The push figures here were
read before the log had a `sync=` field, so they include the wait for the
panel's next TE pulse: 32.3 ms of push and about 4 ms of waiting. `push=` now
leaves that wait out.
A tap on the overlay adds about 16 ms to the push (48 ms). The registered
row's 0.93 MB is from before the QR overlay merged; the same code rebased onto
it was read again at 5.0 fps, a step of 169 ms and a push of 35.7 to 37.6 ms,
with 6,058,235 bytes of PSRAM free (the QR buffers included, so not comparable
with the idle figure). The 20 by 50
variant (`*count: 40`, `*resolution: 50`) is the final code on a later main,
which holds a QR buffer, so its free PSRAM is not comparable with the others.
Its step is 45 percent below the registered build's (91 ms against 165); on
the first-flash code the same smaller scene cut the step by 34 percent (234 to
154 ms). Heap was flat in every capture, and no reset or panic appeared.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

input.command:
python3 - <<'E'
p='.claude/rules/hacks.md'; s=open(p).read()
assert s.endswith("\n")
s+='''- Hexadrop (`hexadrop_single.c`) runs at about 10 fps, under the 15 fps bar.
  Splitting its step on the device showed the maths and the edge walk cost
  0.1 ms and all the rest is canvas writes: about 860 KB of 16-bit stores
  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.
  More needs a shared canvas change or rasterising in row bands.
- Halo (`halo_direct.c`, `halo_planes.h`, `halo_circles.h`) draws whole circles
  into 1-bit pixmaps and XORs two of them. Its pixmaps are packed bit planes
  (27 KB each), not colour pixmaps: 434 KB colour stand-ins made Seuss mode
  (three runs in four) 5-9 fps, because window-sized circles are millions of
  PSRAM writes, and a float circle fill alone changed nothing. A device boot
  is deterministic, so every boot picked Ramp mode and hid that: force
  `*colorMode: seuss` temporarily to measure the other mode. It overrides
  `*delay` to 10 ms (upstream asks for 100 ms), so the circles grow faster.
- StonerView's seven files are built as one unit by `stonerview_gl.c`.
  Upstream never frees its oscillator list ("how do we free this?"), so the
  wrapper frees it through the `next` links before upstream's release.
- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which
  converts four PNGs from `vendor/` into blobs in the build directory: they
  are never committed (1.5 MB of C text each for the large sheets). It
  starts with a typed "trace" sequence, then rain; `*matrixFont: small`
  gives 46 columns instead of 23. Its text modes read no text: the
  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
p='.claude/rules/x11shim.md'; s=open(p).read()
s+='''- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
  pointer no mask is made.
- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
  (default 0). No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and ignores a GC's
  function. Halo handles both inside its own wrapper (`halo_planes.h`).
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
E
markdownlint .claude/rules/hacks.md .claude/rules/x11shim.md 2>&1 | head

Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) during the
Flurry/Halo/Hexadrop/StonerView/XMatrix batch.

## What

Flurry was not ported. It is the one hack of the batch with no branch work.

## Why it was skipped

- It draws `NUMSMOKEPARTICLES` (3,600) blended, textured quads a frame
  (`glDrawArrays(GL_QUADS, ...)` in `flurry-smoke.c`).
- It needs GL that TinyGL here lacks: `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`,
  `gluBuild2DMipmaps` (a 256 by 256 luminance-alpha texture), and the
  luminance-alpha texture format itself.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` cannot read it (it handles single-file hacks), so
  this is arithmetic, not a measurement: with the tool's model of 4 us a
  vertex and 570 ns a pixel, 14,400 vertices are about 58 ms before any
  fill, and blended quads that overlap heavily cost seconds. Well under
  1 fps.

## To decide

- Is it worth trying at all? A cheaper route might be a count of particles
  far below 3,600 through a build-time patch, which changes the look.
- If yes, first teach `gl_budget.py` multi-file hacks so the estimate is a
  number, and measure one frame's fill on the host.

Source: `vendor/xscreensaver-6.16/hacks/glx/flurry*.c`.
E
cat > $S/issue-hexadrop.md <<'E'
Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) during the
Flurry/Halo/Hexadrop/StonerView/XMatrix batch.

## What

Hexadrop is ported and correct but runs at about 10 fps on the device, under
the 15 fps bar.

## What was measured

| Build | fps | step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| As copied (double) | 2.2-2.6 | 377-442 ms |
| Single precision | 3.0-3.2 | 282-313 ms |
| Float convex fill (hack-local) | 9.0-9.2 | 76-79 ms |
| Two-pixel stores (registered) | 10.2 | 64-66 ms |

Splitting the step with a temporary probe: with the pixel writes skipped the
step is 0.1 ms, and with the whole fill skipped it is also 0.1 ms. So the
maths, the edge walk and the sin/cos are negligible, and the rest is canvas
writes: about 430k pixels (860 KB) a frame into the PSRAM canvas, with the push
(32.5 ms) on top. 32-bit stores only moved it 16 percent, so it is not the
store count; the likely cost is PSRAM cache-line fills from many small
scattered row writes (about 480 polygons of about 25 rows each).

## Ideas, not tried

- Record each frame's polygons and rasterise them in bands of about 8 rows, so
  writes sweep memory instead of jumping a row stride per scanline.
- A faster shared `canvas_fill_polygon`: it divides in double per edge per row
  (software maths on the S3). Hexadrop's wrapper has its own float fill, but
  other polygon hacks do not. Shared code, so it needs Rod's say-so, and any
  rounding change would move pinned frames.

The same lesson cost Halo a first attempt (its window-sized circles were
millions of PSRAM writes as colour pixmaps; packed bit planes fixed it).

Code: `firmware/src/hacks/hexadrop_single.c`.
E

## What

Hexadrop is ported and correct but runs at about 10 fps on the device, under
the 15 fps bar.

## What was measured

| Build | fps | step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| As copied (double) | 2.2-2.6 | 377-442 ms |
| Single precision | 3.0-3.2 | 282-313 ms |
| Float convex fill (hack-local) | 9.0-9.2 | 76-79 ms |
| Two-pixel stores (registered) | 10.2 | 64-66 ms |

Splitting the step with a temporary probe: with the pixel writes skipped the
step is 0.1 ms, and with the whole fill skipped it is also 0.1 ms. So the
maths, the edge walk and the sin/cos are negligible, and the rest is canvas
writes: about 430k pixels (860 KB) a frame into the PSRAM canvas, with the push
(32.5 ms) on top. 32-bit stores only moved it 16 percent, so it is not the
store count; the likely cost is PSRAM cache-line fills from many small
scattered row writes (about 480 polygons of about 25 rows each).

## Ideas, not tried

- Record each frame's polygons and rasterise them in bands of about 8 rows, so
  writes sweep memory instead of jumping a row stride per scanline.
- A faster shared `canvas_fill_polygon`: it divides in double per edge per row
  (software maths on the S3). Hexadrop's wrapper has its own float fill, but
  other polygon hacks do not. Shared code, so it needs Rod's say-so, and any
  rounding change would move pinned frames.

The same lesson cost Halo a first attempt (its window-sized circles were
millions of PSRAM writes as colour pixmaps; packed bit planes fixed it).

Code: `firmware/src/hacks/hexadrop_single.c`.

content.text:
Rod, I've ported four of the five hacks. StonerView, XMatrix and Halo clear 15 fps, Hexadrop doesn't, and I haven't attempted Flurry. All 459 host tests pass and the board is flashed with a normal rotating build. The work is on `feature/port-batch-flurry-halo-hexaddrop-stonerview-xmatrix`, 9 commits, local and unpushed, with no PR opened.

| Hack | On the device | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| StonerView | 36-41 fps | No shim gaps. Upstream never frees its oscillator list, so the wrapper frees it (the leak test failed before the fix). |
| XMatrix | 17-26 fps in the rain, 37-87 in the sparse phases | Glyph PNGs are converted at build time from `vendor/`. |
| Halo | Seuss 22-26 fps, Ramp mean 27 | Two attempts, see below. |
| Hexadrop | about 10 fps | Below the bar; issue #71. |
| Flurry | not ported | Issue #70. |

- **Halo:** my first version used colour pixmaps and averaged 15 fps, but that boot was Ramp mode. Device boots are deterministic, so every boot picks Ramp. I forced Seuss temporarily and it was 5-9 fps. Packed 1-bit planes fixed it (about 3x faster), and host frames and the pinned hash are unchanged. It also overrides `*delay` to 10 ms.
- **Hexadrop:** the step is 0.1 ms with the pixel writes skipped, so all the time is PSRAM canvas writes. The shim fills polygons in double-precision maths, which the chip runs in software. A local float fill, single precision and two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with identical frames. More would need a shared canvas change, which I didn't touch, or drawing in row bands.
- **Flurry:** it draws 3,600 blended textured quads a frame and needs GL calls TinyGL lacks. My estimate is well under 1 fps. That's arithmetic, not a measurement, because `gl_budget.py` can't read multi-file hacks. Say if you want it attempted anyway.

I filled the shim gaps needed, each test-first: `XSetWindowBackground`, `GXxor`, `XGetImage` and `XPutImage`, key events and `XLookupString`, Xt timers, and `textclient.h`. I also fixed a shim crash where `image_data_to_pixmap` dereferenced a NULL mask pointer.

I also regenerated the porting assessment, added device rows and gotchas, and kept my usual notes file with the same findings.

**What I need your eyes on:**
1. **Halo's pace:** the 10 ms delay makes the circles grow roughly twice as fast as upstream. Is that too frantic? A longer delay like 30 ms trades some fps for a calmer pace.
2. **Halo colours in both modes:** I measured Ramp and Seuss but judged neither on the screen.
3. **XMatrix:** the large font gives 23 columns, and the corners are clipped by the round display. `*matrixFont: small` gives 46 columns if the large one looks chunky. It opens with a typed "WARNING: carrier anomaly" sequence before the rain.
4. **StonerView:** are the translucent squares vivid, and is there any flicker?
5. **Hexadrop:** the octagons should shrink out to the next colour on a blue and magenta grid. Is 10 fps tolerable, or should it go?

To see the new ones, press the button back from the first hack: XMatrix first, then Halo, StonerView and Hexadrop.

The branch isn't pushed, because you said no PR yet and a push is outward-facing.

content.content:
# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and its
  `assert()` aborts on a failed allocation, and it ran at 1.2 fps, so it is
  shelved (issue #37): its source stays in `firmware/src/hacks/celtic/`, it is
  not in `g_hacks[]`, and `failed_ports.txt` lists it. A failed port that has
  its source and a measured row still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed
  standalone. Measure on the device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/deliver-branch

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `gh pr merge N --merge` once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). His approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire
  Gates check to finish. A stacked PR's gate
  can fail "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges: if approvals
  and findings pass and the PR is mergeable, merge it, with no rebase.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- `entire agent-help` says trails are unavailable; `entire trail create` works.
  Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `tools/assessment_measured.md` (rows, paragraphs and
  the hack count) and the three `build_src_filter` lines in `platformio.ini`,
  as well as the generated assessment. Keep both sides, put the newer hack
  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase
  (the skill PR was reviewed before the Blaster and Substrate code it referred
  to had landed). Check it against `main` before dismissing, and put the
  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers
  have approved" right after a force push, though Rod had approved; his word is
  enough, so say so and go ahead.
The assessment now has a line over 80 characters: my Flurry reason is too long, and it lands in the generated file. These commits aren't pushed, so I'll shorten the reason, regenerate, and amend.

Opened by Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction. Draft until Rod
has approved it.

## What

Four more hacks on the board, the shim gaps they needed, and Flurry marked as
a failed port. Rod has looked at all four on the device and wants to keep them.

| Hack | On the device | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| StonerView | 36-41 fps | No shim gaps; fixes an upstream leak in its wrapper |
| XMatrix | 17-26 fps in the rain | Registered with `*trace: False`: no intro |
| Halo | Seuss 22-26, Ramp mean 27 | Bit planes; `*delay` overridden to 10 ms |
| Hexadrop | about 10 fps | Under the 15 fps bar; Rod: not noticeable |
| Flurry | not ported | Marked failed, issue #70 |

Every copied hack is byte-identical to `vendor/` and has its notices row.

## Shim changes

Each was written test-first, and the new code was mutation-checked.

- `XSetWindowBackground` (used by `XClearWindow`) and the `GXxor` constant.
- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` for 32-bit images, key-event types,
  `XLookupString` (finds nothing), Xt timer stand-ins, a `textclient.h`
  stand-in, and the `XYPixmap` constant.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL mask pointer. It used to crash
  XMatrix on start.
- The window background is reset when a hack stops. Found on the device: after
  Hexadrop, Pyro showed a solid colour. The test failed before the fix.

## Things worth a look

- Halo cannot use the shim's bitmaps, so `halo_planes.h` has its own packed
  1-bit planes. A first version with colour pixmaps measured the wrong mode:
  a device boot is deterministic and always picks Ramp, so Seuss mode (three
  runs in four) was 5-9 fps until the planes. The plane code is tested pixel
  for pixel against the shim's circle fill.
- Hexadrop's step is all PSRAM canvas writes (0.1 ms with them skipped). More
  speed needs a shared canvas change or banded drawing, so it is left for
  issue #71.
- XMatrix's glyph sheets are converted from `vendor/` at build time by
  `matrix_glyphs.py` and never committed, like Pacman's sprites.

## Verification

- Compiles for the device, and runs on it: each hack was flashed, measured
  and looked at by Rod. Flash use is 66.7 percent.
- Host: 460 tests pass, plus 307 Python tests. `check_notices.py` passes.
- Not measured: a long soak with rotation on, or Halo's Ramp mode against a
  recent main. Heap and PSRAM were steady in every capture.

Refs #70, #71.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

content.text:
The one finding on trail 38 is fixed and marked resolved. It was a real bug. The fix is in the working tree, uncommitted, as the skill requires.

**The finding:** Halo creates its GCs with the second colour in the creation mask (`GCForeground | GCBackground`). The shim's `XChangeGC`, which `XCreateGC` goes through, ignored `GCBackground`. So clear bits painted black until Halo's first `XSetBackground` call. I reproduced it before changing anything: asking for `0x5678` read back `0x0000`, in the shim test and in a Halo test.

**The fix:** `XChangeGC` now honours `GCBackground` (`xshim.c`, with the header comment updated). I added two tests, one in the shim and one on Halo's copy path. They fail without the fix and pass with it.

**Effect on Halo:** I reverted the one line temporarily to compare. Without it, the opening frames (8 to 40) had up to 150,000 black pixels. With it, those pixels take the intended second colour. By frame 200 the frames are identical, because Halo's first recolour sets the background explicitly. So only the first few seconds of each Halo run were wrong, which is likely why it still looked great to you.

- **Re-pinned:** Halo's pinned frame hash moved, as expected, so I re-pinned it.
- **Other hacks unaffected:** I re-ran `test_hacks` afterwards so XMatrix and the later pins were checked, and none moved. Pacman, Pedal, Laser, Flame, Mountain and XMatrix also pass `GCBackground`, but none of their pinned frames changed.
- **Tests:** 463 host tests ran, 462 pass now, with the one failure being Halo's hash, which I then re-pinned. The re-run of `test_hacks` passed all 56.

Not re-flashed; I haven't looked at it on the board.

Say "commit and push it" when you're happy, and I'll add it to PR #72.

There's no `CLAUDE.md` in this repo. The checked-in project file is `AGENTS.md`, with area notes in `.claude/rules/`, so that's where these belong. Here is what this session taught that the files don't already say. I've kept it to things likely to recur.

### Update: `AGENTS.md`

**Why:** the `test_hacks` timing is stale (it ran 2m10s to 2m20s every time this session, and the full suite 4m20s to 5m), and the GL-hack count is now out of date.

```diff
-  Gears was the first GL hack; Unknown Pleasures is the fifth.
+  Gears was the first GL hack; Unknown Pleasures is the fifth and StonerView
+  the sixth.
...
-  single-hack tests take about a second); `test_hacks` alone takes about 100 s.
+  single-hack tests take about a second); `test_hacks` alone takes about
+  2m20s and the whole `pio test -e native` about 5 minutes.
```

### Update: `AGENTS.md` (Gotchas)

**Why:** this cost me a failed run (exit 127) and a false alarm about a hung test.

```diff
+- A background command (`run_in_background`) ignores `cd`, so `source
+  tools/env.sh` fails there with exit 127 and "pio not found": give it the
+  absolute path (`source /…/tools/env.sh && cd /…/firmware && pio …`).
+- On a busy Mac (load average over 10) the suite can look hung. Before
+  killing it, `sample $(pgrep -f .pio/build/native/program) 3` shows where it
+  is: it was in Unknown Pleasures, slow but moving.
```

### Update: `.claude/rules/hacks.md`

**Why:** one existing line now contradicts what I measured. It says each device boot picks a new mode, but Halo picked Ramp on all five boots, which matches AGENTS.md's "a boot is deterministic".

```diff
-  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. Each boot on the device picks a new mode
-  too, so measure each mode from separate boots.
+  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. A device boot is deterministic too (Halo
+  chose Ramp on five boots in a row), so a hack that picks a mode with
+  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
+  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the
+  random state differs by then.
```

I left out things already recorded: the probe-flag step splitting, the mutation-script pattern, and the hash-pinning workflow are all in `techniques.md` or `AGENTS.md`. The one-off bugs (Hexadrop background leak, `GCBackground`) are in `x11shim.md` from earlier.

You've said before that `AGENTS.md` revisions go straight to `main` with no PR. Do you want me to apply these three and commit them to `main` that way?

aiTitle: Flurry, Halo, Hexaddrop, Stonerview and xmatrix hacks

input.project_notes:
Batch merged as PR #72 (2026-10-11): Hexadrop, StonerView, Halo, XMatrix on the StopWatch board; Flurry marked failed (#70); Hexadrop speed is #71.

Decisions and why:
- Halo: first built bitmap emulation on 434 KB colour pixmaps. Looked fine (15 fps) but I had measured the wrong mode. Device boots are deterministic so Halo always boots Ramp; Seuss (3 in 4 real runs) was 5-9 fps. Forcing *colorMode: seuss temporarily exposed it. Packed 1-bit planes (27 KB, byte fills) fixed it: 22-26 fps. Plane code is unit-tested pixel-for-pixel against the shim's own circle fill.
- Hexadrop: step split on device with a temporary probe flag: pixel writes skipped = 0.1 ms, so ALL 77 ms is PSRAM canvas writes. Single precision and a float fill got 2.4 -> 9 fps; 32-bit stores only 16% more. Not store-bound; likely cache-line latency from scattered writes. Left as issue #71 (idea: raster in row bands).
- Bugs found AFTER the first review: window background stored on the long-lived Display leaked from Hexadrop into Pyro (fix: reset in xshim_release_pixmaps, test runs Hexadrop then Pyro); XChangeGC ignored GCBackground (trail review finding, real: early Halo frames black).
- Mutation checks caught a real test gap twice (right-edge wrap onto the next row is invisible to ASan).

Shim: XGetImage/XPutImage, key events, Xt timer stand-ins, textclient.h stand-in, GXxor, XSetWindowBackground, image_data_to_pixmap NULL mask fix (crashed xmatrix on start).
input.technical_insights:
- A measurement is only as good as the mode/phase it ran in. Check a side-channel (here PSRAM free = one pixmap vs two) that tells you which code path ran, before trusting a number.
- When a step is slow, split it with a temporary flag that skips ONE thing before guessing. I guessed twice (double maths, then circle maths) and was wrong both times; the probe found writes-to-PSRAM in one run.
- Memory placement matters more than arithmetic on ESP32-S3 + PSRAM: a 16x smaller representation (1-bit planes) beat every maths tweak.
- State stored on a long-lived object (Display) leaks across hacks; reset it where per-hack state is already released.
- A test that stops at the first mismatch in registry order hides later hashes: after repinning, re-run to check the ones after it.
- A loaded machine (load avg 13-16) makes a 2 minute suite look hung; `sample <pid>` shows the process is moving.

He reviews on the device himself and reports concrete observations (Pyro background solid colour after Hexadrop; XMatrix intro). He pre-authorised flashing for the session and said no PR until he says. He asked for uninterrupted batch work with a list of things for his eyes at the end, and appreciated plain reporting of what was unmeasured (Flurry estimate, Halo single boot). His call on Hexadrop: fps not noticeable, keep. Prefers AGENTS.md revisions straight to main. Warm sign-off ("little chum").

Glad the habit of checking numbers against each other paid off before Rod saw a slow Seuss mode. Also pleased the bug Rod found (Pyro) turned out to be a clean, testable cause.

input.content:
🧮 Shipped four xscreensaver hacks onto a tiny round ESP32 display today (StonerView, XMatrix, Halo, Hexadrop) and learned three things worth sharing:

🔬 I "measured" Halo at 15 fps... in the wrong mode. A PSRAM-free figure that didn't add up (one pixmap, not two) gave it away. The common mode was 5-9 fps. Always cross-check which code path your benchmark actually hit.

🧊 Fix: stop faking 1-bit bitmaps with 434 KB colour pixmaps. Packed bit planes (27 KB, byte fills) made it ~3x faster. Memory placement beat every maths tweak I tried.

🪤 Two of my first guesses at the bottleneck were wrong. A temporary "skip this one thing" probe flag found it (Hexadrop: 0.1 ms with the pixel writes skipped, so it's all PSRAM writes) in a single flash.

🎨 Bonus: a colour I stored on a long-lived Display object leaked from one screensaver into the next. State on long-lived things needs resetting when the thing using it stops. 🖤➡️🟦

"""wire.py <name> <Class> <author/copyright text> [<notice name>] [--src DIR]

Copies vendor/xscreensaver-6.16/hacks/<name>.c to firmware/src/hacks/<name>/
and appends the registry entry, the test lists (name, hash placeholder, leak
test) and the THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES row. Appends after the newest hack."""

import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("/Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver")
name, cls, copyright_text = sys.argv[1:4]
notice = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else "jwz permission notice (above)"
src_dir = "hacks"
src = root / "vendor/xscreensaver-6.16" / src_dir / f"{name}.c"
dst = root / "firmware/src/hacks" / name / f"{name}.c"
dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
shutil.copy(src, dst)

p = root / "firmware/src/hacks/registry.c"
s = p.read_text()
externs = list(re.finditer(r"extern const HackEntry \w+_hack;\n", s))
last = externs[-1]
s = s[: last.end()] + f"extern const HackEntry {name}_hack;\n" + s[last.end():]
s, n = re.subn(r"    &(\w+)_hack\};", rf"    &\1_hack,\n    &{name}_hack}};", s, count=1)
assert n == 1
p.write_text(s)

p = root / "firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c"
s = p.read_text()
s, n = re.subn(r'"\};\n  const int n = sizeof\(expected\)',
               f'",\n                                         "{cls}"}};\n  const int n = sizeof(expected)', s, count=1)
assert n == 1
s, n = re.subn(r"(\};\n\nvoid test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main)",
               f"    0x1ull, /* {cls} */\n\\1", s, count=1)
assert n == 1
s = s.replace(
    "int main(void) {\n  UNITY_BEGIN();",
    f'void test_{name}_stops_do_not_leak(void) {{\n  check_restarts_and_stops_do_not_leak("{cls}", 0);\n}}\n\nint main(void) {{\n  UNITY_BEGIN();',
    1,
)
s = s.replace(
    "  RUN_TEST(test_gears_stack_use_on_the_host_has_not_run_away);\n",
    f"  RUN_TEST(test_{name}_stops_do_not_leak);\n  RUN_TEST(test_gears_stack_use_on_the_host_has_not_run_away);\n",
    1,
)
p.write_text(s)

p = root / "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md"
s = p.read_text()
rows = list(re.finditer(r"\| `firmware/src/hacks/[^\n]*\n", s))
last = rows[-1]
s = s[: last.end()] + f"| `firmware/src/hacks/{name}/{name}.c` | {copyright_text} | {notice} |\n" + s[last.end():]
p.write_text(s)
print("wired", name, cls)
